Ninety Parallel Sinusoids with Linearly Increasing Period

A. Michael Noll’s early computer-generated image: ninety parallel wave lines whose period shortens across the sheet, made to approximate Bridget Riley’s Current.

Source
V&A: Photograph, E.34-2011
Creator
A. Michael Noll (computer artist)
Made
1964 (image); photographic print 1970s
Style
Op art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Precise, vibrating, systematic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its print, E.34-2011 (1210 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A describes a photographic print of a computer-generated image first created in 1964, and quotes Noll: “The top sinusoid was expressed mathematically and then repeated again and again. The result closely approximates the op-art painting ‘Current’ by Bridget Riley.” V&A.

Riley’s Current (1964) is the painting reproduced on the cover of The Responsive Eye.

Observed

  • About ninety thin black curves run in parallel across a white sheet, in a block with a white margin.
  • Toward the left the curves are nearly straight; toward the right the waves become shorter and steeper.
  • Where the curves turn steeply at the right, the gaps between them narrow and the lines seem to shimmer.
  • There is no text, no tone, and no colour.

Why it belongs

Noll shows that the Riley effect is a rule: one curve, repeated with a fixed offset, with a period that changes linearly. This makes it the most direct reference for generating op patterns in code.

The image sits where op art meets early computer art, and that link is a natural fit for screen design.

Borrow

Generate an op field from one function: repeat a sine curve with a fixed vertical offset and shorten its period across the width.

Keep a wide white margin around the line block so that the field reads as an object.
